title: Lovász conjecture
formal:
Does every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph have a Hamiltonian path? With the definitions below, prove or refute
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\quad
\bigl(\operatorname{Connected}([n],E)\land
\operatorname{VertexTransitive}([n],E)\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\exists p\in S_n\ \forall i\in[n-1]\quad
\{p(i),p(i+1)\}\in E.
\]
There is no restriction on the number of vertices, degree, automorphism group or representation as a Cayley graph. The required spanning object is a path; its endpoints need not be adjacent. This is an existence assertion without a computational time bound or a requirement to find the path efficiently.
definitions:
Let \(\mathbb N_{\ge1}=\{1,2,\ldots\}\), and write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite nonempty simple undirected graph is a pair \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\) and \(E\) is a set of two-element subsets of \([n]\). Vertices \(u,v\) are adjacent when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). Thus there are no loops, parallel edges, orientations or weights. Using labeled vertices loses no generality because every finite graph is isomorphic to one on \([n]\). A finite representation consists of \(n\) and the \(\binom n2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of unordered pairs; no algorithmic constraint depends on this representation.

The graph is connected if for every \(u,v\in[n]\) there are an integer \(m\ge0\) and vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_m\in[n]\) such that \(v_0=u\), \(v_m=v\), and \(\{v_{j-1},v_j\}\in E\) for every \(1\le j\le m\). A sequence of length zero is permitted when \(u=v\).

Write \(S_n\) for the set of all bijections \([n]\to[n]\). An automorphism of \(G\) is a bijection \(\sigma\in S_n\) with
\[
\forall x,y\in[n]\quad
\bigl(\{x,y\}\in E\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \{\sigma(x),\sigma(y)\}\in E\bigr).
\]
The graph is vertex-transitive if for every ordered pair \(u,v\in[n]\) there exists an automorphism \(\sigma\) with \(\sigma(u)=v\). The automorphism may depend on the pair. Equal vertex degrees alone are not the condition.

A Hamiltonian path is a permutation \(p\in S_n\) such that consecutive vertices in \(p(1),\ldots,p(n)\) are adjacent. Bijection ensures that every vertex occurs exactly once. For \(n=1\), the adjacency requirement ranges over the empty set \([0]\), so the single vertex is a Hamiltonian path. No closing edge from \(p(n)\) to \(p(1)\) is required. A cycle discussed in the context is a cyclic sequence of at least three distinct vertices with edges between consecutive vertices and from the last back to the first; its length is its number of vertices. Such a cycle is Hamiltonian only if it contains every vertex.

For the restricted results mentioned below, a Cayley graph has the elements of a finite group as its vertices and joins \(g\) to \(gs\) for elements \(s\) of a fixed inverse-closed set of nonidentity group elements. A connected Cayley graph is an example of a connected vertex-transitive graph, but the conjecture includes all graphs satisfying the stated symmetry condition. A directed graph instead has ordered edges; results about paths or cycles required to follow those directions concern a different class of objects.

context_blocks.text: The main source explicitly states the Hamiltonian-path conjecture and distinguishes it from the stronger eventual Hamiltonian-cycle conjecture. This card preserves the path question, including the one-vertex graph.

The July revision proves that, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), every sufficiently large connected vertex-transitive graph on \(n\) vertices has a cycle of length at least \(n^{2/3-\varepsilon}\). This sublinear guarantee does not provide a path through all vertices.

The April revision of the dense Cayley-graph paper proves Hamiltonian cycles for connected Cayley graphs of sufficiently large order \(n\) and degree \(d>n^{1-c}\), for some absolute constant \(c\ge1/200\). The Cayley and density hypotheses restrict its scope.

The August directed-graph revision still identifies the undirected Hamiltonian-path conjecture as open. Its directed-cycle examples can miss at least \(n/12\) vertices even in a longest directed cycle, but these are not counterexamples to the undirected path assertion.

A late-August paper again states the general path question as open. Its Hamiltonian-cycle theorem concerns a restricted family with special graph orders and automorphism-group hypotheses, so it does not cover every graph in this card.

why: A resolution would settle a central connection between graph symmetry and spanning structure. A proof would show that connectedness and vertex symmetry suffice for a spanning path across every finite simple undirected graph, beyond particular group constructions. A counterexample would identify an obstruction that survives complete vertex symmetry. The existence question remains meaningful without asking for a fast algorithm.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal assertion, or of its full logical negation, using the finite graph and permutation definitions above.

A positive answer must show that for every \(n\ge1\) and every connected vertex-transitive graph \(([n],E)\), some permutation has all its consecutive pairs in \(E\). It may establish existence without providing a uniformly efficient construction.

A negative answer must establish
\[
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\quad
\operatorname{Connected}([n],E)\ \land\
\operatorname{VertexTransitive}([n],E)\ \land\
\forall p\in S_n\ \exists i\in[n-1]\quad
\{p(i),p(i+1)\}\notin E.
\]
This requires one finite graph satisfying both hypotheses and a proof that every ordering of its vertices fails to be a Hamiltonian path. Existence of the counterexample can itself be proved; an efficient search procedure is not an additional requirement. An arbitrarily long nonspanning path, a spanning result for one subclass, or a counterexample to a directed or cyclic variant does not establish either required conclusion. The target is exact, so numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not relax it.

sentences: A graph is vertex-transitive when an adjacency-preserving permutation can send any vertex to any other vertex.
The Lovász conjecture asks whether every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph has a path that visits each vertex exactly once.
The path need not return to its starting vertex, and the statement includes graphs outside the Cayley-graph setting without requiring an efficient path-finding algorithm.
A resolution would decide whether connectedness and vertex symmetry alone force a spanning path, beyond known long-cycle guarantees and restricted Hamiltonicity results.
A complete Lean answer must prove the path exists for every graph in the stated class or prove that one graph in the class has no such path.
